blocks.text: ᾿Ανθρακίζων τὲρεβίνθου [Anthrakizōn terebinthou] [col. 47] [II, 584] roasting chickpea over the coals. And on the second page of the Ecclesiazusae the Scholiast has: Ὑποπίνοντες ἔκοπτον φρυκτοὺς ἐρεβίνθους [Hypopinontes ekopton phryktous erebinthous], Having drunk rather freely, they pounded roasted chickpea. The Roman writers, too, mention roasted chickpea more than once. Plautus in the Bacchides, Act 4, Scene 5:
I will roast him as thoroughly as chickpea is roasted.
Nor if the buyer of roasted chickpea or of nuts approves of something.

Cassian, Collat. 8, ch. 1: He brought in a basket holding roasted chickpea, which they call trogalia. Τρωγάλια [Trōgalia], that is, sweetmeats. And even today the Arabs call roasted chickpea قلي [qly] kali, as we have just shown ^{(7)}. Accordingly all the Hebrews, on the passage of Samuel we mentioned, recognize two kinds of kali: the former made from grain, the latter מקטניות, from pulses, or ממיני קטניות, from kinds of pulses. So Kimchi, R. Levi and R. Esaias on that passage. And R. Selomo describes the latter kali thus: וקלי ממינים של קטניות מיבישין אותו בתנור כשהן לחין והם מתוקין לעולם וטוחנין אותן ועושין מהם מאכל שקורין שתית, Kali are kinds of pulses which, while still fresh, are dried in an oven; they always remain sweet, and they are ground, and from them is made a food which they call sethith. This is taken from the Talmudic tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 38 a, where we read that Barzillai the Gileadite sent David חרי מיני שתיתאה, two kinds of sethitha, that is, two kinds of kali. And there the Gloss says: שתיתא תבשיל העשוי מקמח של קליות שייבשין בתנור ויש שעושין אותו מקמח עדשין ולפי שהן מתוקין יותר מדאי נותנים שם חומץ, Sethita is a dish made from the flour of kali dried in an oven. There are also some who make it from lentil flour; and because these are excessively sweet (that is, insipid), vinegar is poured on them. It is true that שתיתא sethitha is said to be made from lentils, for in tractate Gittin, ch. 7, fol. 70 a, the Talmud text itself mentions שתיתא דטלפחי, sethitha of lentils. But what is added about vinegar I think is a σφάλμα [sphalma] of the Glossator, who had read somewhere that this dish is made from lentil וחמצא, and chickpea, and understood vinegar instead of chickpea, because in Chaldee חמצא chimtza, chickpea, and חמצא chumtsa, vinegar, are written with the same letters. However that may be, we have amply proved that usnen, or kali, is chickpea or a kind of chickpea. And we have shown why it is called קלי kali: namely because it is roasted or parched. But اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or rather وشنان [wshnān] vvsnen, as many write it, [II, 585] comes from the verb وشن [wshn], which, of land, a camel, etc., means to swell and to stand out. Hence the chickpea is rightly called usnen, because of the uneven angles with which it swells and stands out. For it is not round like the pea, but angular and top-shaped ^{(8)}. But why it should be called sparrows' dung or dove's dung is entirely hidden from me. I only know that it is so called. Nor is there any doubt that the nut Kendem, or Gendem, is called dove's dung for this very reason: that with its grains or little stones it imitates the shape of the chickpea. For it is a granular earth, like chickpea, as the old translator of Avicenna has it, in the place cited above.
